speechtext:
that the bill be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure today, a long-awaited pleasure I might say, to lead off the third reading debate of Bill C-84 which will authorize the sale of Petro-Canada shares to the public. Allow me first, if I may, Mr. Speaker, to take this opportunity to thank members from all sides of the House who have taken part in the various stages of debate on this bill. In particular, let me thank the members from both sides of the House who were part of the legislative committee on Bill C-84 who I believe carefully and thoughtfully studied the various clauses of the bill.
I appeared twice before the committee and many witnesses appeared and gave testimony. The evidence is overwhelming that the government is on the right track and is doing the right thing in privatizing Petro-Canada.
Opponents of this bill have expressed concerns about Canada's energy security in the context of Bill C-84. These concerns are quite natural and understandable given the recent volatility of world energy markets. I believe that we have been able to demonstrate that Canada's energy security does not depend on continued government ownership of Petro-Canada. The security of supply can be reached in many other ways. The government has the ability to do that. Through all stages of debate on this legislation, the government has been able to give Canadians the assurance that Canadian energy security is not at risk as a result of public participation in the ownership of Petro-Canada.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, in addressing the legislative committee, outlined the government's energy policy in words that bear repeating. He said, and I quote:
-current policy emphasizes primary reliance upon the operation of competitive markets for decisions regarding energy supply, demand, pricing and trade. The government considers that competitive prices provide the most appropriate and effective signals to both investors and consumers. We know, from the experience of the early 1980s, that such a market-oriented approach is far better, both in economic terms and in terms of federal-provincial relations, than policies which emphasize heavy reliance upon regulation and government intervention.
The privatization of Petro-Canada is perfectly consistent with the government's energy polity as stated by the Minister of Energy. I might say that I just returned from the west after pre-budget consultations with a number of interested groups and organizations, two of which were involved dramatically in the energy business. They all have said that the energy industry over the last four years has done a tremendous amount of work in streamlining its operations, getting themselves in shape without the vagaries, if I can use that terminology, of subsidies and offering them this here and that there. They have told me that their capital expenditures for next year are going to increase rather dramatically in exploration and capital costs. That is very good news not only for the west, I might say, although the west would benefit from it the most, but also from ridings such as mine, where I have 52 companies that I have identified within the riding of Brampton that supply the oil patch with needed goods and services. When the energy industry is doing well, all of Canada benefits. I can assure you of that.
December 18, 1990

A privatized Petro-Canada, strengthened by a new equity infusion, will be able to contribute to Canada's long-term energy security by continuing its ongoing exploration and development activities, thereby increasing the strength of the Canadian oil and gas industry. That is what Bill C-84 is all about; strengthening Petro-Canada so it can get on with the job of doing what it does best and that is exploring for and developing Canada's energy reserves and contributing in a positive way to Canada's future energy security.
Mr. Speaker, I want to quickly reiterate for all members of the House the two main reasons why the government is moving forward with this initiative. First, government ownership of Petro-Canada is no longer required to fill a public policy role.
Second, the company needs an infusion of capital in order to allow it to participate in the exploration and development of Canada's oil and gas reserves. For this reason, the initial public offering will be comprised of treasury shares enabling the company to raise much needed equity.
As I have said on numerous occasions, the privatization of Petro-Canada will be good for the company and good for Canadians. We recognize the important role that Petro-Canada has played in Canadian oil and gas development and the special relationship that the company enjoys with Canadians across this country.
The bill in no way diminishes these two important roles. Neither does it diminish the government's ability to carry out its energy policy, to ensure energy security and to promote environmentally sound practices within the Canadian oil and gas industry.
I must say that the Canadian oil and gas industry has been very understanding and very co-operative and has worked extremely hard in the field of environment and, as a matter of fact, has been recognized by environmental groups for the work that it has done. This, in no way, is going to change that in the importance of environment to all 2,500 to 3,000 energy companies we have in this country. The rules, the regulations, the goals and the aspirations all remain the same and privatizing Petro-Canada is not going to have a negative effect on the environment whatsoever.
Government Orders
As a matter of fact, by privatizing Petro-Canada, by allowing the company to raise equity from individual Canadians rather than relying on taxpayers, we are providing the company with the means to become an even stronger presence in the Canadian oil and gas industry, and we are strengthening the Canadian identity of the company by inviting individuals to buy shares.
I hear the opposition saying that we own it now. Well, I submit that the taxpayers have had all the liabilities and none of the benefits from the company. It is on our books now for $4.3 billion. Therefore, who really does own it? The government lays claim to it but there is a tremendous debt attached to that.
The legislation opens new opportunities for Petro-Canada. With the ability to raise new equity it can get on with that job that it does best, exploring and developing our gas reserves. I think most important, as we saw in the Air Canada privatization, a wide distribution of shares and restriction on their ownership will give Canadians a real and direct interest in the future of the company. These ownership restrictions will also ensure that control of Petro-Canada will remain firmly in Canadian hands.
I have sat through the debate. I listened intently to the opposition claims. There are ideological differences between the New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party and the Progressive Conservative Party on this particular issue. The polls I have seen indicate that the majority of Canadians are in favour of privatization of Petro-Canada as long as it is kept in Canadian hands.
I see my hon. friend from Toronto over there shaking his head, indicating no. If he is privy to information that I do not have I would be very happy to see it, but the record shows that security of supply and owning a state oil company does not go hand in hand unless the state oil company owns exclusively all the oil in the country. As a matter of fact, Petro-Canada accounts for only 6 per cent of the upstream activity. The other 3,000 energy companies account for the rest.
So, it is very important to understand that Petro-Canada, although playing a very important role, primarily in marketing because it has 19 per cent of the market in the downstream activities is one of many players in the energy industry. It is time that it it set free so that it can expand without having to come cap in hand to government for funding. Now it can go to the private sector for

Government Orders
funding. It can raise it through the normal means of financing these companies similar to its competitors and at the same time remain in Canadian hands.
There are numerous changes being made in this country. If you listen to the opposition day after day after day, they do not want anything changed. They want it all to remain the same. They do not want us to economize. There is not one area of the economy where we have had to economize because of a fiscal situation, and we have had to make cutbacks in many, many areas there is not one area where they have agreed that we should cut back. Not one. Neither the Liberals nor the New Democratic Party. They want it exactly the way it was.
Well, the world is moving very quickly. We have seen changes that no one could have predicted two, three or four years ago. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this government has kept up with those changes and is leading Canada into the 21st Century as a progressive country, not one that is constantly playing catch-up, but one that would be right up there leading in the economies of the world. That is what this is all about. That is what change is all about. We can no longer sit back and ignore these changes that are taking place in the world, as much as the opposition would like to. At least that is what I am hearing from them. Do not cut VIA Rail. It does not matter that people do not ride it, do not cut it. Do not cut the CBC, just give them more money. We give them $1,034,000 now, give them another $110 million. That is their solution to all the problems of the country, to give more, more, more. It does not matter what issue it is. If we are talking about structural changes within our economy, they oppose that. They want to go back to the old ways.
Well, in 1984 the Canadian people made it extremely clear that they did not want to go back to the old ways. They were not happy with the old ways. Change was coming and they needed a group of men and women who could bring that change forward and that is what this government is doing. Some of them are difficult decisions. Some of them cost us dearly in the popularity polls we see published monthly. Tough decisions have to be made and this government and the Prime Minister who leads this government is prepared to make those tough decisions and stick with them because we know in the
long-run that they are going to be for the good of the country.
I can even say that former Liberal Cabinet Ministers understand that times change and we have to look at things differently today than we did 15,16 or 17 years ago when the NDP forced the Liberal government into creating a Crown corporation known as Petro-Canada.
As recently as six weeks ago, the hon. Marc Lalonde, the former minister of energy, a former finance minister and, I guess, a former everything in the former government led by Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, was interviewed on the Gzowski show as part of a panel. He was there with Rosemary Brown from the New Democratic Party and, I believe Dalton Camp was representing the Progressive Conservative Party. It was a regular roundtable that they had discussing what was going on in politics.
One day the subject was the privatization of Petro-Canada. I know my colleague, the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources will refer to this later in the debate today. What he said at that time was: "No, I am not opposed to the privatization of Petro-Canada". His opinion was that Petro-Canada has served its purpose and now it is time to get on with the change that is taking place, that it is not a window on the industry any more. We have organizations within governments now that have the ability to collect all the information necessary to know what is going on in the energy industry.
Rosemary asked him if Petro-Canada was not there to control energy prices. Marc Lalonde said that it was was never envisaged to control prices in this country. That was never one of its mandates. One would think from listening to the New Democratic Party that that was the reason Petro-Canada was there, to control prices. They stand up and say: "Why does Petro-Canada not lower oil prices or gas prices at the pump?" They do not care if it loses money, but say: "We'll prop them up with subsidization from government." That is not the way it should work.
The socialist ideas around the world are being thrown out. Privatization is taking place in every country of the world by governments of every political stripe, including the communists, the socialists, the liberals, and the conservatives.

It is not an ideological thing. It is a common sense thing. The New Democratic Party says: "It's ideological, it's a Conservative bent." It is Conservative philosophy because it works, but it is being adopted by communist countries and by members of Socialist International, to which the New Democratic Party belongs.
One of the interesting things is that a number of these countries are coming to my department for advice on privatization and how they would enact privatization in their countries. We have had them from Australia, New Zealand, and Venezuela. Members of my staff on the privatization side of my department have been in Poland and Czechoslovakia providing advice on privatization. It is happening around the world.
Mexico has privatized something like 260 companies since President Salinas has taken over. He knows it is right. He knows that is the way to go, that governments can no longer pour billions and billions of dollars into these Crown corporations to keep them afloat, and that it is totally irresponsible to the taxpayers of the country.
Privatization is a fact of life. Crown corporations, yes. There are certain Crown corporations we need. I have never denied that. There are certain services of government that must be provided by government. I have never denied that. There are services that the private sector cannot or will not provide that must be provided. Governments have to provide them. That is why many of these Crown corporations came into being, but they have outlived their usefulness.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the House today as the lead-off speaker on behalf of the Official Opposition at third reading stage of the Petro-Canada privatization bill.
It is with a little sadness, on this side of the House, that we embark on this task. It is our last chance to change our minds and to save what was and what could be in the future a valuable Canadian institution which has languished over the last few years as a result of the absence of government leadership.
There are two things that strike me about the way we have begun this privatization. The first is the haste with which the government has addressed this. If we recall, the matter was first placed before the House of Commons on October 1. That was about two and a half months ago. There have been a lot of other bills around the House which have been here a lot longer than two and a half months.
I have only been here since 1988.1 could be wrong, but I cannot recall another bill that did not have unanimous approval zipping through this House as quickly as this one has. I think that is unfortunate because, aside from the simple procedure of selling off, we also have a recognition of the issues surrounding the thrust, reasons and policies of privatization. It is long past time when Canadians must begin to address the issue of privatization.
This government has embarked upon a long series of privatizations. I would concede that one privatization by itself would not make a trend or would not make or break the future of this country, and we could live with that. In fact, I would have to concede, as I am sure most members of the House would, that there is the odd enterprise which can be privatized and not materially impair the many other policy goals that the government has and should have. For the record, and so we will know the extent of privatization, I will mention a few by name.
We have had de Havilland, Canadair, Nordion, Route Canada, CN Hotels, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Northern Canada Power Commission and Northern Transportation Company. The sale prices for these are all in the many millions of dollars. I say that only to indicate that there is a large volume of money involved here. It is not simply a sale of a few excess Crown assets such as paper clips and the like. There was Northwest Tel Inc., which is a CN subsidiary; Pecheries Canada Inc., Teleglobe for half a billion dollars; Terra Nova Telecommunications, another CN subsidiary; Canada Development Corporation, Fishery Products International, Nanisivik Mines Limited and Theratronics International Ltd.
There are other smaller interests which I will not mention, interests that the government acquired by taking as security for loans and financings. The list is a very, very long list and what it should serve to show all of us is that we have not got a simple one-time privatization, but what we have is a long string of dismantling

of enterprises which for the most part-not in every case-were put in place to serve Canadians, not just Canadians in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto but Canadians all over the country.
The way in which this government is proceeding with these privatizations, I fear that we are taking a lot of sand out of the sandbox. When you take sand out of the sandbox and get down to a certain point, the kiddies will not want to play any more. They do not regard it as a sandbox. It is just a box. If the government proceeds on this ideologically-driven-and I maintain it is ideologically driven-course of privatization, it will succeed in selling out, but we will have left for all of us a geographic shell without Canadian presence. That drive to divest Canada of these institutions and corporate enterprises, to me, manifests a bankruptcy in the pursuit of policy.
The government sees that there is no Canadian goal that must be accomplished and therefore sells off the vehicle.
I am a temporary resident of Ottawa in my responsibilities as a member of Parliament and I represent a riding in Scarborough. Canadians living in major cities such as Vancouver, Montreal and Halifax, are surrounded in our urban environment by many, many institutions. You cannot leave your house without tripping over them; sidewalks, sewers and stop signs. But these cities only represent a part of Canada.
There are the people who do not live in the urban areas like Ottawa, who are not surrounded by all of these national institutions like Parliament, like the grandiose city halls. They are working people who do not get a chance to see, participate in, or pursue goals that are related to these Canadian institutions. That is one area where this government has missed the boat. It has forgotten that it must provide to Canadians in every region, not just to the concentrated pocket of voters in urban areas, leadership in institutions, a presence, a reason for feeling for being Canadian.
The Minister has just told the House that Petro-Cana-da did not serve any public purpose. Well, we all know that is true. The only reason, however, that Petro-Cana-da did not serve a public policy purpose was because the
Government Orders
government took it away in the first place in 1984. It removed it. It publicly required Petro-Canada to pursue profit-oriented enterprise with no public policy mandate, and that is not the reason why Petro-Canada was created in the first place.
It is very easy for the government to say that Petro-Canada does not fulfil a public policy purpose. It could not possibly do so because the government sucked that out of Petro-Canada in 1984.
I have also noticed how the government has changed the semantics of privatization as it pursues its goal of privatization. When the thrust of privatizing began 10 or 20 years ago it was called selling off or divestiture, then it became privatization. But that term has not sanitized it enough, so now we have the euphemistic titles of this and other bills where the process is called public participation.
What would constitute public participation in an enterprise more than a Crown corporation? How could you get any more public than that? Have we gone full circle? Public participation, the way it is discussed in relation to the government's privatization initiatives, means selling shares on the market. That is not the only perspective on public participation that we have in this country, so why the drive to sanitize? Why does the government have to change what it calls it? Well, I submit it is because there are some ugly truths that lie behind divestiture, sell-offs, sell-out, privatization.
We like to call it participation. It is not going to fool anybody. It is not hard to sell off. This is the easiest initiative this government has ever had to undertake. It is really easy for a liquidator to come in and sell off the corporate asset-any asset.
All you do is take it and hold it out in the marketplace for the best price you can get. In fact, you do not even care what price you get because you as a liquidator get a commission. That is what every broker or underwriter obtains when that group participates in a divestiture, a sell-off. I do not knock that. They are doing their work. But boy, is that easy. It is a dead end policy if all we are going to do is sell, sell, sell. Where does it end? I suppose in the end there is nothing left.
Will there be a post office? Why not sell it?

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Good idea.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
My friend opposite says good idea. I am afraid we differ once again. I think a lot of Canadians will differ with the hon. member. However, there is lots of time to discuss, as long as the government does not tiy to ram it down our throats in another two and a half months.
What will happen to the CBC? Who knows. We will wait for the new agenda. Unfortunately for the government, that Ronald Reagan-Margaret Thatcher neoConservative agenda that was there, led by an eminent politician from the United Kingdom who is no longer with us as Prime Minister, is disappearing. I feel that the government has lost its true leader in this. As it embarks on other potential privatizations, it is going to find itself not knowing where it is going. That is when Canadians will take notice.
Everyone in this House knows that the opposition stands in fundamental disagreement with the privatization of Petro-Canada. For that reason, it has been a little tough at committee and in the House being constructive about a sell-off because once it is sold, it is gone. It is not there any more. That makes it tough.
It is also tough to show that you are opposed and then be required to put forward a constructive amendment to make the sell-off better. I do not know if you can make a sell-off better, but a number of members at committee tried to do that. We addressed several issues. I am going to repeat them here so that the record will show the areas of sensitivity that we have to address in the House of Commons and in committee in this particular privatization. Some of these themes pertain to other privatizations as well but these are the Petro-Canada ones.
One of them had to do with the Canadianization policy. That was one of the driving forces that gave rise to Petro-Canada's birth, Canadianization. We in the early days of Petro-Canada were very fearful as Canadians that our petrochemical capability and the energy capability related to that were being managed by non-resident corporations, the seven sisters. We were quite concerned. I remember the time very well. For whatever reason now perhaps we are not so concerned. I do not know why. I am still concerned. In any event, Canadianization was one of the driving reasons. Canadianization is still a policy of this government. The energy minister
stated very clearly, very honestly at committee that it was.
If we look at the foreign ownership provision contained in this bill, and there is one, it says that non-Canadians can own up to 25 per cent. It does not say they will own 25 per cent. It says that they can own up to 25 per cent. It is simply logical for me to submit to the House that the Canadianization policy thrust of this government has now just been reduced with reference to Petro-Canada by 25 per cent, potentially. Let us take off a mark in this government's pursuit of its Canadianization policy. It has one strike against it there.
There is a relationship between that provision and the free trade agreement. When this government negotiated the free trade agreement it secured a concession that permitted this government to sell a Canadian enterprise or Crown corporation and to maintain the Canadian ownership. It went to the length of securing that in its negotiation of the free trade agreement. The provision says that once we do privatize-and I am paraphrasing-whatever level of foreign ownership is put in place at that time is the lowest threshold that we can ever impose.
Therefore, hypothetically, if there is a change of heart in relation to this legislation a year or two or three from now, under the free trade agreement, if we stay true to the agreement and if it is fully implemented, we will never be able to require Canadian ownership of greater than 75 per cent. Once we cross this bridge it is finished. We cannot go back. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the House.
We also dealt with the prospect of a piece of Petro-Canada, which under the current provisions could not be greater than 10 per cent, being purchased by a foreign state. I thought it would have been fairly obvious to members in the House and in committee that we would not want a foreign state to own a piece of what was our national oil company. I guess it was too complex to deal with that because the amendments proposed to preclude a foreign state or agency from owning a piece of Petro-Canada were not passed.
We can only hope that we will not as a Parliament have to deal with an issue in the future-and it will be a public issue; it will be a headline in the newspaper-where a foreign government or agency of that government or a state oil company of another government purchases a piece of Petro-Canada because it thinks it has a good
marketing opportunity or a good outlet for its oil. I am talking about one of the mid-east oil companies, Venezuela, or our friends in Mexico. Maybe Canadians will not mind. I just feel we should have addressed that in this bill, and we did not.
Dealing with the area of strategic assets, when Petro-Canada is gone we will have sold a vehicle, a tool or a piece of machinery that should have permitted us to address petrochemical energy supply problems in this country. Petro-Canada is a company that has facilities from the east coast to the west coast.
I believe that the legislation should have permitted us to prevent Petro-Canada from selling or disposing of an asset that our government believed was strategic in purpose and objective, at least for as long as the government held shares in Petro-Canada. This would include the disposition, sale, liquidation, bankruptcy, dismantling of means of distribution of petrochemical supply or a refinery or a pipeline, any asset.
I agree that would be a burden on the shareholders of Petro-Canada, but it must be remembered, and the people who buy these shares have to remember where Petro-Canada came from. In that period of transition, from the sale of the first share to the sale of the last share, they know that we in government and they with their private investment have one foot on the dock and one foot on the boat. They know that now, because we are not selling Petro-Canada all at once. We are doing it in segments and tranches over a period that might run up to ten years. We do not know.
In any event, our ability to address the need for retaining strategic assets is not in the bill.
I agree we have had a healthy discussion on official languages. I agree with the minister. In my view and in the view of most of my colleagues, the provisions in the bill dealing with our official languages, French and English, within the Petro-Canada enterprise are not adequately dealt with. The bill provides that Petro-Canada would be the arbiter of how it will dispense its goods and services in both languages. It will decide.
That criteria, that mechanism that is contained in the articles of incorporation and I am a little confused as to how an individual in Canada who is not a shareholder of Petro-Canada, just a consumer, the guy with the chain
Government Orders
saw that I referred to earlier, can deal with the issue of official languages in Petro-Canada.
It is no good to say that this is a private corporation, let them do whatever they want. The government has already seen the need to address official languages in the act. It is in the act. I say if you are going to address it, do it right. Do it comprehensively. The recommendations of the Official Languages Commissioner, Mr. Fortier, were rejected.
There was some discussion of another provision dealing with accounting and the Auditor General and it had reasonable debate in committee and in the House. But I am of the view, given the difficulties the Auditor General has had and obstacles he has encountered in obtaining the true financial information regarding the acquisition of Petro-Canada, those obstacles will still be there when he, as part of his responsibilities, pursues, investigates or monitors this particular series of sale transactions. Do not even suggest to me that he will not want to do so. This is the largest privatization, divestiture in Canadian history. Our Auditor General is going to be right there watching it.
The Minister of State for Privatization has told the House that the Auditor General and all of us will have access to the prospectus filed with the various securities commissions around the country. That is true, but the Auditor General is not concerned with the prospectus. The Auditor General will be curious about the movement of the money from the underwriters through to the government and what happens to it after that. I am very sure that if cabinet discussions involving the accounting for those moneys takes place, our Auditor General will not have access because of cabinet confidentiality rules. That is not true. I am speculating, but I have seen problems that the Auditor General has had before. I have no reason to believe that it will be different in the future.
I am not suggesting the government will intentionally try to cover up anything. I am simply saying that our Auditor General needs access, and there were amendments proposed to provide that access subject to commercial confidentiality necessary to protect Petro-Canada.

December 18, 1990
Government Orders
As the words of the song go, "You don't know what you've got till it's gone". As sure as I am standing here, this issue will come back to haunt us later, after it has gone. This is, practically speaking, an irreversible step.
I noted just a few days ago an article in The Globe and Mail dealing with the shutdown of the pipeline from southern Ontario to Montreal. It said that there was a plan to shut down this pipeline which carries, I understand, conventional light crude in 1991. That is about two weeks away. I suggest that is a very significant matter because, as the headline says, Quebec would depend totally on imported oil after the closing of that pipeline. Petro-Canada does not have anything to do with this particular pipeline. I am not suggesting it does.
However, we have a decision being made in relation to a pipeline which may mean after its shutdown Montreal would be cut off from Canadian sourced crude. The government has yet to express an opinion on it, but I believe that means of delivery of crude is important to Montreal just as Petro-Canada's role in delivering energy supplies in various parts of the country is important to Canadians.
Once it is gone it is gone. Once Petro-Canada decides it wants out of the refining business in a particular location, once the refinery is gone, it goes into the hands of individuals who may shut it down, mothball it, or use it for something else that may not be consistent with our national interest as seen by the National Energy Board.
They are not the only sources of capital. For equity capital, yes, we have to sell the shares, but we have other institutions in this country that finance themselves otherwise. The two most obvious examples were the monopoly electrical utilities in Quebec and in Ontario. As is already in the record of the debates, these utilities have debts in the $20 billion range.
On the same day as the pipeline issue was in The Globe and Mail there was an article about Ontario Hydro and its financing needs. It did not have a problem going back to the market. Petro-Canada in the first crunch wants about $750 million. Ontario Hydro in 1991 is going to raise $4 billion. Its bonds were very hot, snapped up in the marketplace. In fact, I think it was able to reduce the interest rate a little bit. They were snapped up, $1.25 billion. I think it took a few days or a week but the issues were all snapped up.
I know that Petro-Canada would prefer to have equity capital because it is cheaper. The dividend pay-out might be in the vicinity of 4 or 5 per cent when dividends are payable, whereas debt capital costs in the vicinity of, in the case of the Ontario Hydro rate, 10.25 per cent. In any event, the other financing options included preferred shares, special shares with a guaranteed rate of return plus participation. They could have been sold to the private sector and the control over Petro-Canada as a state oil company could have been maintained. In any event, we are trying to make a silk purse out of a sow's ear. We cannot do it.


The government says it has mechanisms in place to deal with energy issues of national importance. I am waiting to see what this institution, or series of institutions such as the National Petroleum Monitoring Agency can do if they can do anything. Are they toothless wonders? I shudder to think that they are simply sham institutions set up to show Canadians that we have this pretence of action. I do not know, but I am skeptical.
The issue of the financing of Petro-Canada came up. Were there any alternatives to going to the private sector? We all know that there were, but Petro-Canada executives were of the view expressed publicly that the private sector, the marketplace for common share security, was where they felt they had to go now and in the future.
Just a few moments ago the minister indicated, with reference to a quote of the Hon. Marc Lalonde, that Petro-Canada was never intended to control prices. That is true. No one on this side of the House ever suggested Petro-Canada's role was to control prices. Why does he suggest that that was the case? No one suggested that Petro-Canada was a monopoly and would control prices. It is a player, it is a participant in an oligopolistic petrochemical industry so that we know automatically that Petro-Canada has an influence on price. It does not control price and no one ever said it did. No one ever said it should. It was our window on the price setting mechanism. It was not control. It is unfair of the minister to suggest that that was the intention. He is putting words, intentions, he is attributing these things to the opposition when that just is not true.


Yesterday in debate at report stage, the minister and other members suggested that the birth of Petro-Cana-da came about because it was ideologically driven. There is some ideology lying behind all of us in this House. We are not stupid. It is not as if we do not have any ideas. Of course, there was some ideology behind Petro-Canada. What did I hear in this House from the opposite side? I heard the minister a few moments ago admitting that there was conservatism, if I can use the term-he used it, small c conservatism-lying behind the drive to privatize. Therefore, the privatization of Petro-Canada is just as ideologically driven as was the move that gave birth to it, if it even was. I am not sure that it was ideology which gave birth to Petro-Canada.

Since the 1984 federal election, the Conservative government has tried to whitewash its actions by using all kinds of euphemisms like divestiture, dismantling, privatization and public participation. And the debate on this bill is no exception.
Mr. Speaker, let me tell you that although the Conservatives may try to disguise their privatizations, Canadians like me know perfectly well this is about killing Canadian initiatives that have served Canadian interests well. Openness and integrity are definitely not part of this government's character.
Mr. Speaker, the Mulroney government must take the responsibility for killing Canadian initiatives in the energy sector.
This bill to privatize or divest Petro-Canada makes no sense at all, especially at a time when we are facing a critical energy situation and when a full-blown energy crisis could flare up in the Middle East. This is not the right time to consider selling a fundamental instrument of our energy sector. If the government succeeds in privatizing Petro-Canada, we will lose our window on the industry, an industry now controlled by foreign interests. This means that Canadians will have no presence that will protect and defend our interests in this crucial activity sector.
The big oil multinationals will now be able to call the shots. I fail to see why this government has tried to rush through this legislation. Bill C-84 was introduced on October 1, and after only a few days of debate, the
Government Orders
process is now almost finished. I think there are some serious contradictions between this government's policies.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80 concerning firearms was introduced in June, and today, this bill is nowhere near coming into force.
I tried to discuss this in the legislative committee as well as in the House when I introduced some amendments, but unfortunately, my motions and those of my colleagues were voted down.
Paragraph 9(l)(e) describes the provisions requiring Petro-Canada to ensure that any member of the public can communicate with its head office and obtain available services in either official language, where Petro-Canada determines there is significant demand. The problem is that it is up to them to determine whether there is significant demand or not.
There is no provision for the eventuality that Petro-Canada ignores the provisions in its articles concerning official languages. These provisions, which relate to certain aspects of services in official languages, appear only in the articles, which practically no Canadian will ever see.
And even if a Canadian citizen were acquainted with these provisions and felt that they were not being observed, I wonder whether this Canadian citizen would have any way of making Petro-Canada respect these provisions. The people to whom these articles apply are the corporation's agents. Other Canadians will have no recourse.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, this government's privatization policy is more important than respecting Canada's two official languages and the rights of Canadians in this respect. This was clearly demonstrated by a refusal to consider suggestions made both by the Commissioner of Official Languages and myself and my colleagues, concerning respect for official languages rights.

Mr. Speaker, we do not run Canada for a profit. In fact, we do not run it, but Canadians do not run it for a profit either. Our job is simply to make this country work, to make it live, to give it direction, to give it purpose. That is our job in the House of Commons and that is the job of every Canadian who holds a position of leadership in his or her community.

The step this government is taking in the privatization of Petro-Canada is one of a chain of privatization initiatives and it is one which we believe is irreversible. What Canadians want is a government which cares and feels for Canadians in every region of this country, not just in the urban centres; a government that knows what is necessary in all of the regions to create a country that has a healthy economy and a purpose.
We on this side of the House want to participate in achieving that goal. We believe that the government-

Mr. Speaker, I regret the intervention by the hon. member, just as I was reaching the pinnacle of my remarks, the conclusion of my scintillating remarks. As a result, I will resist the temptation to go back to the beginning of the conclusion.
This debate should crystallize the views of Canadians with respect to the continuing policy of this government in divesting, getting out, selling out, privatizing public participation, whatever is meant by that.
I also cannot abandon this portion of my remarks without noting that the government felt it necessary to introduce and use time allocation at each stage of the bill. The government says-and if I am wrong I am sure government members will correct me-that the reason it had to be done was to catch the marketplace in the spring. That may be true. The government may have wanted to, but I do not think Canadians wanted the government to catch any marketplace. It is regrettable that the debate did not permit many members to address, not just the privatization, but the long sequence of privatizations and the effect they are having on the institution of government in the country and the perception of Canadians that the government is leading in a precise direction that will provide prosperity and unity to
all of the country. I urge all members in the House to vote against this bill at third reading.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tory minister of state for ideology earlier said that Petro-Canada did not serve any public purpose. Well, this Conservative government does not serve any public purpose at this moment. I only wish that it would go, and go quickly.
In debating this bill at third reading, I have to go back and think about the way it was in 1972-73, in the early seventies, when there was what was called an energy crisis, brought on by the Arab embargo. At that time, there was no Petro-Canada and those who owned the oil industry in the country were predominantly foreign. Ninety per cent of the energy sector of this economy was foreign-owned. In fact, it had all the answers. It had its books and it kept its books close to its chest.
In Canada, we were faced with the problem of the National Energy Board not knowing what the inventories of energy were in the country. The government had no ability to go into the books of the private oil companies to examine what was going on. The oil companies were giving erroneous figures to the government. They were skittish. They would not put any investment into exploration.
At that time, Canadians and the government were concerned about what was called energy self-sufficiency. In fact, the common phrase used was: "Let the eastern so-and-sos freeze in the dark", and it became the language of bumper stickers. We all recall that.
I would say that, at that time, ideology had little to do with the establishment of a national oil company. Petro-Canada was formed at that time, I would say, not so much from ideology, but more from the economics of the situation at the time.
There was a desire on the part of the government of the day, which was a Liberal minority government supported by the NDP, to establish a national oil company and Petro-Canada was formed. If I recall, the Conservatives fought that every inch of the way. They went to the wall opposing it. The man who became Prime Minister shortly after it was formed, the hon. member who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, called it a white elephant at the time, if I recall correctly. In fact, he went down to defeat in 1979. He went down to

defeat because he attempted at that time to privatize Petro-Canada. That was one of the causes of his defeat.
Petro-Canada was established and it became an integrated oil company from well-head to gas pump. Canadians began to identify with their oil company. We know that Canadians spent in 1990 some $6.8 billion to build up Petro-Canada.
We have to ask ourselves why we established Petro-Canada? First, we wanted to have a window on the industry. That was the phrase at the time, a window on the industry. We Canadians and the Government of Canada had to have the information. It had to know what was going on in that sector because if any government was to plan economically, it had to have that important information because energy is at the very basis of economic activity.
Second, we wanted to have a leverage point in the energy sector because 90 per cent of that sector was foreign-owned. Petro-Canada was an attempt to start putting Canadians on the scene of ownership in the energy sector.
A third reason was to discipline other oil companies, not to set the price, but to prevent Canadians from being gouged in times of what were called energy crises. In fact, today I suggest that if Petro-Canada was not in the field, the gouging would be even greater than it is right now.
A fourth reason that has become even more apparent today, given that total PR job of a so-called green paper, is a public policy purpose.
Petro-Canada had four reasons and I have to ask myself if those reasons are still valid today in 1990. Do we still need to have a window on the energy sector? Do we still need to have a leverage point in the energy sector? Do we still need to be concerned about disciplining the other oil companies, and do we need to make that a public policy instrument? Yes, now more than ever Petro-Canada justifies its existence as a publicly-owned corporation.

ment is attempting to do to Petro-Canada, if it succeeds with the vote today to dismantle Petro-Canada, is to send a signal to the world that Canada no longer has a government that is a guardian of our national heritage.

speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The message is clear. By getting rid of Petro-Canada, we consume our children's inheritance. We are destroying a symbol of national pride. That is what they are doing.
Second, there is this window on the industry. A considerable amount of knowledge has been gained by the government through its oil company about how that sector works. It has given the government an expertise which it never had before, an expertise that is important and information that is important for any government concerned about planning the economy of the country. Petro-Canada is certainly not a corporate welfare bum. It pays its way.
The other question is the leverage. Selling off Petro-Canada starts moving foreign ownership in the energy sector back up. It will go up to 60 per cent if the government is successful in selling off Petro-Canada.
As for disciplining other oil companies, in my view Petro-Canada has certainly minimized the greed of the oil companies. Every time there is a crisis they move in very quickly and take advantage of the roller-coaster prices and get the benefit of windfall profits. Wait until the books are reported for this year. We will see massive windfall profits that will make the banks look like a kindergarten in the way of profits. Petro-Canada is a brake on those oil companies who are out to gouge Canadians. There is no doubt in my mind.
Then, there is the public policy purpose. If ever there is a time for a national oil company to serve a public policy purpose, now is the time. The government is bereft of any kind of practical, specific environmental strategy. The green plan is simply a public relations exercise.

December 18, 1990
Government Orders
Petro-Canada can be used in a very practical and specific way with respect to the environment. One, we have suggested that we can use Petro-Canada stations to recycle ozone-depleting CFCs from automobile air-conditioners. Petro-Canada can do that by setting up reclamation centres at its stations. It can recycle used engine oil. It can promote alternative energy resources, for example fuel ethanol from grain. It will give the grain farmers a more solid income base and, of course, there is employment to be gained in that activity. Petro-Canada could be promoting research and development, and commercialization of alternative energy sources, such as solar and wind power.
In other words, Petro-Canada becomes an active participant. It becomes an activist. It plays an activist role in researching and developing these alternate approaches to energy.
Surely, the whole idea is not to keep on consuming non-renewable fossil fuels. Surely, the role of a national energy company, owned by the taxpayers of Canada and built up with their investments, is a legitimate public policy purpose for a national oil company. I believe that that is what Canadians want their oil company to do, not to be so-called sold off after having written down the book value of its assets.
Imagine this. My colleague here knows all about these things. He is a tax lawyer. If I came to him for advice, what would he tell me if I said: "Here, I own this oil company. Energy prices are going up through the ceiling and we are into an energy crisis. Is this the time that I should write down the value of my oil assets?"

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is shameful.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
He says it is shameful. Of course, it is shameful.
Mr. Speaker, can you imagine not even in any tidy bookkeeping way of getting maximum money? You do not write down the value of your assets when you are holding an asset that is in demand at this point in time. The government is doing that. It wrote it down to $1.8 billion.
I will deal with these Tories in a minute. I will deal with them.
There is another reason for keeping Petro-Canada in public hands. That is because all the profits made by Petro-Canada stay in Canada.
In the 1980s the private oil companies transferred $7 billion of their profits out of this country, $7 billion. The taxpayers of this country spent $6.8 billion in 1990 building this company and the government is prepared to sell it all off. You know something, the taxpayers will not get one penny of that. Not one penny of that will come back into their pockets. All the previous exercises in ideological sell-offs and privatizations have not resulted in one penny coming back into the coffers of Canada because they gave it all back to the companies that were just sold off. We will never see one penny. We are going to sell off our birthright and we are not going to get one penny back.
The next question is a logical one. Why does the NDP oppose this, and is there still a purpose for Petro-Canada? That is the first question.
The next question is an even more important one. Why would the Tories sell off Petro-Canada? Why would they do that? That is the question. Why would they? I suggest to this House and to Canadians watching that the Tories are selling it off because they are locked into an ideology, and that ideology is a corporate agenda. It seems to me that that is what they are doing. Let us face it. Who brought these people into government? Who brought them? Their corporate friends, their big greedy corporate friends. They brought them in here.
Imagine. I want you to imagine it. Here are the Tories after they came to power in 1984 having a banquet, and who do they invite to sit at the table, to draw up at the table? They are eating; they are getting a meal. They are gorging themselves on this meal that is Canada. First, Air Canada-

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in being able to speak to this particular motion and to respond somewhat to what my friend from Nickel Belt had to say.
He made quite an exercise of rewriting history. I mean, talk about a revisionist, he really did characterize it all the way. He says Petro-Canada was formed because of the embargo of 1972-73. I think we have to go back a little further than that. We have to go back to the election of 1972 and Mr. Trudeau's campaign when the slogan was "The land is strong". That campaign slogan got him a minority government and Mr. David Lewis-Oh, do not leave now, come on, you have to get the correct version of history. Come on, John, stay here.
Then came the New Democratic Party rump over there which thought it had the balance of power. In fact, it probably did because Mr. David Lewis was negotiating with Mr. Trudeau on how the government agenda should develop during that minority government. So Mr. Trudeau naturally wanted his close friends and soul brothers the socialists to work together with him on the government agenda. He met with Mr. David Lewis, that successful labour lawyer from Toronto, all those run down at the heels people in the socialist party. Mr. Lewis is one who did quite well.
He made a deal with Mr. Trudeau and said, "We will co-operate with you but the price is going to be pretty steep. You will have to enact some of our agenda and our agenda is to have a Crown corporation known as Petro-Canada, the window on the industry". It really had little to do with the oil embargo. It had more to do with a few needs that the Liberal government had at the time. Talk about a dependency, we were not so much dependent on the Arabs at that time as Trudeau was of the socialists at the time. That is where the dependency was. It was not an oil dependency, but a political dependency at that time. So, Petro-Canada was bom.
My friend says that Petro-Canada pays its way. What a way to pay your way. Does he remember the Canadian ownership tax that the government imposed on the Canadian people? Now there was a cool $1.65 billion handed over to Petro-Canada. Now would not another company in Canada love to have a gift of $1.5 billion just to start out, a little bit of petty cash to start out with. That is the way Petro-Canada pays its way.
Now, he talks about leverage in the sector. We saw the leverage when we had the National Energy Program with 25 per cent back-in provisions. When a company could confiscate the resources of any other company, that is what you call leverage. It had leverage imposed on it by Mr. Trudeau's government. We do not need that kind of leverage in a marketplace.
So my friend has revised history a little bit.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO THE LATE MGR. ALBERTUS MARTIN
TRIBUTE TO THE LATE MGR. ALBERTUS MARTIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of the riding of Drummond were saddened by the news of the death of Mgr. Albertus Martin, who passed away last Sunday. He had been the spiritual leader of the diocese of Nicolet for nearly 40 years.
A highly cultivated and intelligent man, with the class of the most prominent clergymen, Mgr. Albertus Martin compelled recognition at all levels because of his exceptional personality and his humanist approach to the basic problems of this century.
Be it with his flock in his diocese or sitting on Vatican II in Rome, he relentlessly devoted all of his energy and his remarkable scholarship to propagating the Catholic faith. He was renowned not only as a pastor with avant-garde ideas, but also as a great builder and an informed manager.
His death leaves a great empty space, but also the memory of a full life devoted to the advancement and edification of a Church more accessible to the people, a Church in tune with its members and their aspirations for surpassing themselves.
Monsignor Martin, you will not be forgotten!

Mr. Speaker, today the Canadian Association of Food Banks released preliminary figures from its 1990 Hun-gerCount showing that half a million Canadians rely on food banks each month, up 30 per cent from last year.
These figures should be especially distressing because this government continues to follow the same policies it has in the past. We can expect another large increase in the HungerCount next year.
What will happen when UI runs out early for thousands of people, thanks to Bill C-21? What will happen when Bill C-69 squeezes money for vital social programs? What will happen to thousands of low income Canadians when the inflationary effect of the GST is felt?
The answer to these questions is that more and more Canadians will sink deeper below the poverty line and more will be forced to rely on food banks to feed themselves and their children.
I urge this government to rethink and reverse these totally unacceptable policies which are forcing low and middle income Canadians deeper into the mire of poverty.

Mr. Speaker, the decision to cut 18 positions and several programs at the

CBC in Moncton will hit at the very heart of the Acadian community in my riding. The cancelled shows are TeleDebat, Spec-Art, La Revue and Bulletin de Nouvelles Dimanche Midi.

The minister has stated that regional programming would be strengthened by the cuts. In fact CBC cannot maintain minimal levels of programming. Radio-Canada from Moncton services the entire Atlantic region. At a time in our country's history when so many Canadians feel disenfranchised, we can ill afford these cuts.
Acadians need to maintain strong cultural and linguistic links. The dollars saved compare little to the cost of maintaining this heritage.
CBC links our region into the wider information network of Canada. The minister must restore the necessary funding to ensure that minimal regional programming is available.

Mr. Speaker, as Christmas approaches, I ask members of this House to remember a family in Edmonton who are living in a substandard house. Let us just call this family the Smiths.
The Smith family is large, needs a five-bedroom home, but cannot find an affordable one, so it rents a draughty nine-year old house with no hot water.
The affordable government subsidized house that would be available is occupied. It is occupied by the New Democratic member of Parliament from Edmonton East. This New Democratic member lives in a five-bedroom government assisted home and pays only $622 per month. His salary is five times that of the Smith family.
This is outrageous. It is scandalous. The New Democratic member for Edmonton East should hang his head in shame.

Recently, they claimed that the presence of asbestos fibres in certain federal buildings in Ottawa was endangering their health at work, and that it might adversely affect certain workers engaged in renovating the buildings.
A team of researchers from several countries, whose findings were published by Harvard University in 1989, does not agree, and I quote: "Average levels of airborne fibres inside buildings where material containing asbestos is found are extremely low, and the health risk as a result of the presence of asbestos in the buildings is minute, both in absolute and relative terms".

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in Quebec City, after the submission by the Leader of the Liberal Party, the Hon. Jean Chretien, the

federalist option regained lost ground. While the Prime Minister prefers to sit on the sidelines in these debates on the Constitution and national unity, the Leader of the Liberal Party leaps into the fray.
All Canadians saw yesterday that the man who will lead the fight to safeguard and unite our country and defend the rights of all citizens is none other than Mr. Chretien. Mr. Chretien roused his audience by calmly analysing the economic, social, cultural and political realities facing our country, including Quebec.
The Liberal Party knows very well that unprecedented changes are about to took place in this young country of ours, and we intend to meet these challenges.
Jean Chretien wants these reforms to ensure we will have a united Canada, based on co-operation, friendship and pride.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to remind the House, and especially the Minister of Justice, that the end of the GST debate means a new beginning for the fight against criminalization of abortion.
With Bill C-43 about to resurface on Parliament's agenda, the Minister of Justice should consider this. A new survey released by the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists suggests that her attempts to build credibility with Canadian doctors have failed and have failed badly. Even after the minister's 10-page letter to them trying to alleviate their fears, more physicians than ever-almost half the number now performing abortions-say they will stop that service if it is criminalized by this government.
I therefore call on the Minister of Justice to reaffirm, to restate, to repeat her promise of two months ago not to proclaim Bill C-43 as law until Canadian doctors, in her own words, "feel comfortable with it". Right now they do not.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the CBC president and board for
recognizing that we live in times of restraint and that we have to cut the cloth according to the pattern.
However, I do take issue with certain choices they made in making their cuts. In particular, I urge them to reconsider their decision to cut the unique regional program Land and Sea. No other program more effectively shows the economic and social life of Atlantic Canada.
CBC President Veilleux, in announcing these cuts, said that the CBC would move away from local broadcasting and concentrate on regional and national programs. This makes sense to me. However, surely cutting a program like Land and Sea goes against this guideline.
As for local station cuts, why start with smaller stations in communities with no alternative service? Surely more money would be saved and the objective of leaving local service to the private sector more effectively served by leaving stations in places like Sydney, Comer Brook or Windsor to the last and by cutting first stations in places like Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver where alternative local stations exist.

Mr. Speaker, family violence is a social problem and a serious crime. The federal government has a key role to play in the fight against this plague. Housing is a precious tool in such situations, for it can be a shelter for women and children. This is the kind of assistance offered by the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation through "Project Haven".
To help the 25,000 women and children who are mistreated every year, $22.2 million have been set aside to provide 500 housing units. These funds are available to private non-profit groups and Indian bands seeking to create shelter homes by erecting, renovating or transforming existing buildings.
Mr. Speaker, 178 housing units have been promised. I urge all provinces, municipalities and communities to support this measure. The federal government has done more than its share to assist the victims of family violence and will maintain this policy.

In the debate over Quebec's sovereignty, many individuals are trying to frighten Quebecers. Mr. Chretien is one of them. He wrongly maintains that a sovereign Quebec would be in a bad position. He maintains that in a soveriegn province Quebecers will have to cope with their share of the national debt.
Does he mean to say that Quebecers are not now affected by the federal debt? Do they live at the expense of the rest of Canada? I suggest that Jean Chretien has missed the point altogether. Quebecers already shoulder their heavy share of the deficit and the huge debt. It is precisely because they have no control over mismanagement and waste that they want to be sovereign.

Again, Mr. Speaker, the residents of the Gaspe area have been saddened by the loss of three young men. The fishing
boat Bout de ligne with three people on board, Normand O'Connor and Gino Cotton of Riviere-au-Renard and Roger Reeve of Anse-au-Griffon, made its last radio contact at 1 p.m. on Thursday, December 13. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the House will join me in expressing our heart-felt condolences to the relatives of the victims.

Mr. Speaker, we all know that Allan MacEachen is a wily political strategist who gave the impression that he and his Liberal senators and the Liberal caucus were against the goods and services tax. But was he really?
Did he defeat the GST when leave was sought in the Senate to introduce the goods and services legislation? No, he did not. Did he defeat the goods and services tax legislation when it was read a first time? No, he did not, in spite of the fact that the Liberals had a majority in the Senate. Did Allan MacEachen and his majority Liberal colleagues defeat the GST at the second reading stage when the principle of the bill was dealt with? No, they did not. Did Allan MacEachen and his Senate colleagues defeat the goods and services tax when it was in committee for April, May, June, July, August, September and October? No, they did not.
In other words, on numerous occasions the Liberals in the Senate had a majority to defeat the GST but they chose not to. The hon. member for Hamilton East, on April 2 in Winnipeg, said about Mr. Chretien that perhaps he was implicitly supporting the GST. I suspect she was dead on.

Mr. Speaker, as the Christmas season approaches and our thoughts in this Chamber return to our homes and our families, we
December 18, 1990

cannot cease to be aware that murderous tensions exist in our world even as we look upon the season of peace.
In the Baltic states things have worsened considerably in the past few weeks. Nine bombs have exploded in Latvia over the last two weeks, three bombs yesterday alone in Riga, at the Prime Minister's office, the Red Army office and at Communist Party headquarters. Latvian Canadians believe that this is a set-up. They believe it is being done to justify future strong arm tactics by the Soviets.

Canada must be a voice for restraint and for peace in Latvia.

Does the minister really believe that up to 226,000 lost Canadian jobs are mere underbrush and how many more Canadian jobs must fall before the minister comes to his senses?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. Over the weekend the United States gave Canada an unrealistic deadline as to whether we would or would not participate in the U.S.-Mexico trade talks.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a short while ago The Ottawa Citizen put veiy succinctly in 12 words what I think is the whole feeling with respect to Bill C-84 before the House today. It read veiy simply: "Selling Petro-Canada: wrong time, wrong reason, wrong price, wrong decision". We on this side of the House agree wholeheartedly with that statement.
We heard today, at second reading and in committee, what the sale of Petro-Canada would mean to Canada. We have heard very little about what is Petro-Canada. Let me just emphasize again what this great Canadian corporation really is. It has over 7,000 Canadians working in all of its areas. It has over 3,500 retail outlets where we in this country buy our gas and oil. It holds over 6.9 million hectares of land. It has a production capacity of over 22,000 cubic meters of oil a day and for crude oil and liquid reserves it has a reserve of over 92 billion cubic meters. It has natural gas production of 13.7 million cubic feet per day, and in those reserves in natural gas alone, almost 100 billion cubic meters.

In the year just ending, it had $94 million in profit. Its cash flow, expenditures and reserves, its cash end over its expenditures exceeded $600 million. Its revenue was $4.8 billion. It only has a long-term debt of $1 billion, compared to net assets of over $8.5 billion. Petro-Canada is not only a very healthy, vital company, it is a company that well deserves to stay with the original shareholders for whom it was founded, each and every citizen of this country of ours. Every Canadian should remain a shareholder of Petro-Canada.
Petro-Canada was conceived in 1973 and its genesis came because of the terrible problems we were having in this country to be self-sufficient in oil, particularly with the problems we were experiencing in the Middle East at that time. Those problems then subsided and the world market supply of crude oil and natural gas became constant again, until 1979 when we again experienced another crunch in the oil and gas industry with events in Iran of hostage taking and other events that led up to the problems of 1979-1980.
We now experience the severe problem with respect to the availability of crude oil in our country due to what is happening with Kuwait and Iraq and the world situation, particularly the Middle East.
While some may think these countries are far away from the national scene, every Canadian experiences the problem. It comes home immediately when they get their bill for heating their home every month, or they drive up to the pumps to fill up their cars with gasoline. We all know what the experience of Canadians has been in the last two or three months when gas bills for transportation are in excess of 25 per cent of what they used to be and we see what is happening to the cost of heating homes today.
It would be a tremendous expense to the average household in the country to be without transportation, without gasoline or fuel to heat our homes adequately in this climate of ours.
The mandate given to Petro-Canada when it was created in 1975 provided the Canadian people with the power and the will to exercise control where the country was most vulnerable. What we really tried to do in 1975 was to provide security of supply. Through the creation of Petro-Canada at that time, we wanted to ensure that Canada would always have the security of supply of the vital gas and oil that is so necessary in our country. That
Government Orders
was the aim of Petro-Canada at the time; to make Canada independent of any other country in the world and to provide its gas and oil.
It was also created, as we heard from my colleague today, as a window on the industry. We know that the multinational companies which control the oil and gas companies in the world sometimes do not have pricing policies that reflect the needs of a community and of a nation. We thought and expected Petro-Canada to be a window to ensure that the pricing policies for a litre of gas, a gallon of gas or what it cost for a cubic foot of gas to heat our homes, would always reflect something that was tolerable and something with which all Canadians could live. That was another vital reason for the creation of PetroCan.
Another of its three fundamental mandates was to have Canadian control over those vital resources that we in this country need so badly, control over our gas and energy sources.
Those are the three mandates. We had five objectives with those mandates. Petro-Canada was to undertake to explore and develop new sources of energy; to carry out research and development projects relating to all types of fuel; to import, produce, transport, distribute, refine and market hydrocarbons; to produce and distribute and transport other types of fuel, not only for the time when PetroCan was formed in 1975, but for the future availability of whatever energy source we would find.
The fifth objective of PetroCan was to assist Canadian companies, companies other than PetroCan to go into joint ventures, to help finance and provide research funds so that we in this country could be self-sufficient in this vital area that is so necessary to our future economic viability.
In essence, Petro-Canada which was paid for by every Canadian, was intended to look after our national energy interests and the security of our economy in times of crisis as well as in good times. I suggest we failed to do this.
I remember with pride-and I am looking at my friend across the way-the introduction of Petro-Canada in 1975. There was a 2 cent per litre charge put on every litre of gas-
